## Context

Area-based measures are the main instrument states have for conserving marine
biodiversity in place: marine protected areas (MPAs), other effective area-based
conservation measures (OECMs), fisheries closures, shipping measures and the
wider family of area-based management tools (ABMTs). In the Arctic they are
established under a mix of national jurisdiction, regional bodies and global
frameworks, and they have grown up piecemeal — measure by measure, sector by
sector, country by country.

Two things have changed the demand on that patchwork. First, the
Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework's Target 3 commits parties to
effectively conserving and managing 30% of coastal and marine areas by 2030,
through ecologically representative, well-connected systems of protected areas
and OECMs. Second, the Arctic itself is changing: sea ice, the habitat that
structures much of the region's biodiversity, is retreating and thinning, and
the distributions built around it are shifting.

Together these make a pan-Arctic, evidence-based view of area-based measures —
what exists, what it covers, and where the gaps are against ecological
objectives — a practical necessity rather than an academic exercise.

## The project

ACTAME (**A**rctic **C**onservation **T**ool for **A**rea-based **M**easures
and **E**cosystems) is the tool being developed by the joint PAME/CAFF project
running from 2025 to 2027. It is carried out under the PAME Marine Protected
Areas Expert Group (MPA-EG), jointly with CAFF, and led by the Norwegian Polar
Institute.

The project's aim is to give the Arctic Council working groups, national
authorities and the wider Arctic research and management community a shared,
documented spatial basis for discussing where area-based conservation measures
should go — and to make the evidence behind that discussion open, traceable and
reusable.

The first case study is on **sea-ice-dependent species**: the group for which
the link between a physical driver, a habitat and a conservation objective is
most direct, and for which a spatial planning approach has the clearest
near-term value.

## Approach

ACTAME builds on the approach taken by the CCAMLR **Weddell Sea MPA Phase 2**
(WSMPA2) planning tool, which paired an open spatial data compendium with an
interactive interface so that the evidence underpinning a proposed MPA could be
inspected by anyone taking part in the negotiation. ACTAME applies that model to
the Arctic:

- **Document everything.** Each spatial layer carries its own record — the
  conservation objective it speaks to, its resolution, coverage and period, the
  analysis behind it, and its source.
- **Separate data from interface.** The atlas is generated from a metadata
  table, not hand-written, so that adding or revising a layer is a data edit
  rather than a redesign.
- **Work in the open.** The dashboard is an open-source R package; the layers
  and their documentation are published alongside it.
- **Build for the circumpolar view.** The map works in the polar projections
  the Arctic is actually mapped in, so that pan-Arctic patterns are visible
  without the distortions of a global projection.

## Components

| Component | What it provides |
|---|---|
| **Atlas** | An interactive compendium of the spatial layers: what each shows, why it matters, how it was made, and the maps themselves. Filter by objective or layer group, or search the full text. |
| **Map** | An interactive circumpolar map with area-based measures and ecological boundaries as toggleable layers — Large Marine Ecosystems, the CAFF boundary, Exclusive Economic Zones, Ecologically or Biologically Significant Areas and Marine Protected Areas. |
| **Metadata** | The same layer documentation as a searchable, sortable and downloadable table, so layers can be traced, cited and reused outside the tool. |

: {tbl-colwidths="[20,80]"}

The circumpolar basemaps come from the [Arctic SDI](https://arctic-sdi.org/)
and the Norwegian Polar Institute, in six North Pole LAEA projections and polar
stereographic respectively.

## Phases

::: {.card-row}
::: {.a-card .green}
[Phase 1]{.step}

### Horizon scan and scoping
Identifying the conservation objectives the tool should support and the spatial
layers needed to support them — the scoping exercise that determines what the
atlas must contain.
:::

::: {.a-card .green}
[Phase 2]{.step}

### Data portal and atlas
Assembling, documenting and publishing the layers, and building the interface
through which they can be inspected. This is the phase the ACTAME dashboard
belongs to.
:::

::: {.a-card .green}
[Phase 3]{.step}

### Spatial planning application
Using the assembled layers for prioritisation and scenario analysis across the
pan-Arctic domain — moving from *what is known* to *what follows from it*.
:::
:::

## Status

::: {.status-note}
**Early build.** The Map component runs on real data. The Atlas and Metadata
components carry a placeholder skeleton — a small set of example entries and
schematic figures — so that the structure can be reviewed before the project's
own layers are available. Milestones and releases will be posted on the
[Tools](tools.qmd) and [Outputs](publications.qmd) pages.
:::
